name: Thymosin beta-4
summary: A natural 43-amino-acid repair protein used for injury recovery; tested as eye drops and a skin gel with mixed results, it is not approved and differs from TB-500.
what_it_is: Thymosin beta-4 is a 43-amino-acid protein first isolated from calf thymus and found in blood, saliva, tears and wound fluid. Inside cells it binds actin, a building block of the cell skeleton, and in several animal models it speeds skin repair. A drug company has tested it in people as eye drops (RGN-259) and as a skin gel (RGN-137). FDA stresses that TB-500, a short synthetic peptide based on one part of it, is not the same substance.

evidence.why: Human evidence is mixed: the eye drops narrowly missed significance in an 18-person cornea trial and missed their main goals in larger dry-eye and cornea trials, skin-gel wound trials gave inconsistent reports, and the evidence for injury recovery comes from animal studies.

status_us.label: Not approved; eye drops in phase 3 trials
status_us.note: No thymosin beta-4 product is approved. Its eye-drop form, RGN-259, has FDA orphan drug designation for neurotrophic keratopathy; a European phase 3 trial missed its main goal in 2025, and results of a mostly US phase 3 trial were expected in November 2026.

benefits.claim: In neurotrophic keratopathy, a rare nerve-related cornea disease, persistent corneal wounds healed by 4 weeks in 6 of 10 people on the eye drops versus 1 of 8 on placebo, narrowly missing statistical significance in a trial stopped early for slow recruitment; a later European phase 3 trial missed its main goal
In dry eye, a 72-person phase 2 trial and three phase 3 trials in more than 1,600 people missed their main goals; some symptoms, such as discomfort and grittiness, improved in secondary analyses

Skin-gel trials in 71 people with pressure ulcers and 72 with venous leg ulcers found it well tolerated; the developer reported no significant improvement in complete healing of pressure ulcers, while a later summary described faster healing
In 30 people with epidermolysis bullosa, a fragile, blistering skin disease, wounds tended to heal better than with placebo by day 15
Faster skin-wound repair in several animal models, including aged mice

risks.risk: Long-term safety is unknown: the eye-drop and skin-gel trials were short or small, and although they reported no serious drug-related side effects, longer use has not been studied
Possible cancer concern: thymosin beta-4 drives new blood vessel growth and plays a role in tumor progression in research studies; its effect on existing cancers in people is unknown
Immune reactions: FDA says injected peptides may pose a significant risk of immune reactions
Mix-ups with TB-500: FDA says TB-500 is not the same substance, so findings for one do not apply to the other

avoid_if: Current or past cancer, unless a cancer specialist advises otherwise (linked to blood vessel growth and tumor progression in research)
Athletes subject to anti-doping rules (WADA bans thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives)

before: General health check (complete blood count and metabolic panel) if a clinician is involved
labs.why: Thymosin beta-4 has been studied in people only as eye drops and skin gel in trials, so no evidence-based monitoring exists for other uses.

studies.title: Thymosin beta 4 ophthalmic solution for dry eye: a randomized, placebo-controlled, Phase II clinical trial conducted using the controlled adverse environment (CAE™) model
studies.finding: The main goals, corneal staining and eye discomfort, were not met; some secondary measures of discomfort and staining improved, and no safety issues arose.

studies.title: RGN-259 (Thymosin ß4) Ophthalmic Solution Promotes Healing and Improves Comfort in Neurotrophic Keratopathy Patients in a Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Masked Phase III Clinical Trial
studies.finding: Complete healing at 4 weeks in 6 of 10 on the drops versus 1 of 8 on placebo (p=0.07); healing differed significantly two weeks after treatment ended, comfort improved, and no significant adverse effects were seen.

notes_for_editor: Kept separate from tb500 as FDA instructs. Status: SEER-3 (Europe) missed its primary endpoint per a July 2025 trade report [2]; SEER-2 (41 US and 9 EU sites) finished patient visits on August 26, 2026, with topline results expected November 2026 [1]; re-check before publishing. Orphan designation is reported by a Korean news outlet [1], not confirmed on FDA's database. The dry-eye program (ARISE-1 to -3, more than 1,600 people) missed co-primary endpoints, and in 2022 FDA said the results did not support a BLA [5]; ARISE-4 was being prepared. Skin-wound evidence conflicts: the developer's own 2009 release said the pressure-ulcer trial showed no significant difference in complete healing or healing rate [6], while a 2019 journal column summarizing a review said topical thymosin beta-4 accelerated healing in the pressure and venous ulcer trials and reported the epidermolysis bullosa trial of 30 as a trend [7]; the primary trial papers were not opened. The SEER-1 abstract was read through a BVS record because PubMed/PMC/MDPI full text was blocked; the strength was removed from its title. The developer's venous-ulcer release (2009) reported safety and an earlier start of healing at the middle dose, without healing rates; not cited because of the 10-source cap. Compounding: thymosin beta-4 does not appear on FDA's May 14, 2026 503A nominations list (checked, https://www.fda.gov/media/94155/download; not cited for the same reason). The cancer concern rests on a 2007 review of angiogenesis and tumor biology [9], not on human reports. No human data on injected thymosin beta-4 beyond a 14-day phase 1 safety study mentioned in [4].
